I don't like the title for this; it isn't so much that the research is "false" as it is that the conclusions that are made from the data aren't always going to be reproducible when the systems are complicated and nonlinear. In some select cases you can carefully control your experiments in the lab to account for every conceivable variable, but in most experiments in subjects such as biology you can't possibly do that. It is a common thing for experimenters to do the exact same protocol in a biology lab and get a different result due to variability in the test subjects.

I think it is more productive to talk honestly and openly about the limits of science especially when it comes to drawing conclusions based on highly variable nonlinear systems in fields such as biology, sociology, etc.than it is to just label all scientists as charlatans and throw them under the bus.

If you cannot, by the nature of the field being studied, apply the scientific method then it needs to stop being called a science. Calling social studies 'social sciences' gives it an air of authenticity that is wholly undeserved. I am not talking about real charlatans who are merely generating data to promote their non-scientific political agendas or business interests. In reality, this is actually a genuine problem with real scientific studies where the goals are apolitical (like cancer studies to give one example). You can apply the scientific method perfectly and that still does not mean your results will hold true in all cases or that your interpretation of the data is the correct one. For example, you can try your method on one cell line and get a positive result even after reproducing it several times, but when you try it on another cell line you don't see the effect at all. This may not have anything to do with flaws in your method, but could be due to differences in the individual cells themselves (their DNA isn't identical, etc.), or even subtle differences like the first experiments were done in the summer and the second in the winter, etc.

Medical doctors have to grapple with this issue all the time as for some patients a medication will work with no perceivable side effects, but for others it may have harmful side effects to the point where it is worse than the original issue they were trying to address. It sucks, but this is the price we pay for having variety in our lives. The real question is how to address this issue? I think it may be a good idea to start letting scientists in these fields publish more "negative results" so that people can get a better idea of which questions are still open in science and which ones aren't. A good experiment that shows that an earlier conclusion isn't always going to hold true can be just as useful as one that reveals a novel new discovery.
